title: A Case for Process
author: Honest Office
summary: This article argues that the relentless organizational pursuit of efficiency misses the deeper value of process itself — the structured, sometimes friction-filled mechanism through which real work gets done. The author contends that process is not bureaucratic overhead to be minimized but rather a generative tool that surfaces unknown problems, builds the relationships trust requires, and keeps organizations responsive to learning rather than locked into premature solutions. Three distinct benefits of a process orientation are developed: the discovery of what we don't know we don't know, the building of relationships necessary for genuine innovation, and the preservation of organizational responsiveness. Efficiency-first cultures treat collaboration as a cost and optimize their way into brittle systems that lack the relational infrastructure to adapt. The author does not reject efficiency as such but insists it works well only when answers are already known — when conditions are messy or evolving, process is not the obstacle but the path.
points: Process surfaces what we don't know we don't know: efficiency assumes the formula is already written, but process keeps open the question 'Is this actually serving us?' and resists premature optimization.

An over-indexed focus on efficiency inadvertently treats relationship-building and human coordination as costs to be minimized, hollowing out the trust infrastructure that enables teams to surface hard truths early.
Slowing down through process is often precisely what speeds up good outcomes — the friction of structured collaboration is information, not waste.

Organizational responsiveness depends on the capacity to learn; process maintains that capacity where pure efficiency-seeking destroys it by cutting the feedback loops needed to detect and correct errors.
Market responsiveness is itself a product of process, not its enemy — cutting process to accelerate often destroys the adaptive capacity that keeps organizations viable over time.
quotes: Process is the actual mechanism through which work gets done. It is the thing through which people figure out what they need to solve, and the thing through which teams become—imperfectly and sometimes painfully—something more than just a group of individuals in the same room.

Efficiency, as a goal, keeps asking one question: how do we get there faster? But process, if we allow it to serve as the wonderful tool that it is, reminds us that the work of getting there is not inefficiency to be eliminated, but information, relationship, and possibility to be channeled into something meaningful and sustainable.

With a process orientation, we open ourselves up to a friction, which, despite the discomfort it produces, can lead to discovery. Through process, we allow people to ask, 'Wait, why are we doing it this way? Is this actually serving us?'

Sometimes too much of a focus on efficiency can inadvertently result in relationship-building and collaboration being viewed as costs to be minimized. We may not say this outright, but we might as well every time we make someone's workload so insane that they can't step out for a bite to eat with a colleague.

Isn't it the back-and-forth, the space for misalignment to be worked out together, what builds the trust that allows a team to truly innovate and succeed? Are these not the spaces where people share uncomfortable truths early enough, before they become crises?

The teams and organizations that weather uncertainty and change aren't usually the ones that optimized hardest in the good times. They're often the ones that, through their processes, built the muscles of learning and adaptation.
